'''''Heracleum sphondylium''''', commonly known as '''hogweed''' or '''common hogweed''', is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] in the carrot family [[Apiaceae]], which includes [[fennel]], [[cow parsley]], [[ground elder]] and [[Heracleum mantegazzianum|giant hogweed]]. It is native to most of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, but is introduced in North America and elsewhere. Other common names include '''cow parsnip''' (not to be confused with ''[[Heracleum maximum]]'' of North America). The flowers provide a great deal of [[nectar]] for [[pollinators]].

==Description==
[[File:Apiaceae - Heracleum sphondylium-6.JPG|thumb|Close-up of ''H. sphondylium'' flowers]]
[[File:Heracleum sphondylium fruit.jpg|thumb|''Heracleum sphondylium'' fruit]] 
[[File:Heracleum sphondylium (Thomé Bd.3 1905, BHL-81509, Tafel 451) clean, no-description.jpg|thumb|upright|Drawing of ''Heracleum sphondylium'', showing the heart-shaped [[schizocarp]] (fruit)]]
''Heracleum sphondylium'' is a [[herbaceous]], [[flowering plant]]. It is a tall, roughly hairy plant reaching up to {{convert|2|m}} in height. The hollow, ridged stem with bristly hairs arises from a large tap root. The leaves can reach  {{convert|50|cm}} in length. They are once or twice pinnate, hairy and serrated,<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2019|title=New Flora of the British Isles |page=864 |edition=Fourth|publisher=C & M Floristics|location = Middlewood Green, Suffolk, U.K.| isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref> divided into 3–5 lobed segments.

''Heracleum sphondylium'' is most commonly a [[polycarpic]] [[perennial plant]],{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991|pages=235,245–6}}{{sfnp|Zych|2006}} not a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] as sometimes claimed.{{r|Tutin 1980}} The flowers are arranged in [[umbels]], either flat or slightly convex, {{Convert abbreviated|4-25|cm}} in diameter, usually with 10–25 hairy, somewhat unequal rays, each {{Convert abbreviated|2-12|cm|4=1}} long. Each flower has five white or rarely pinkish-white to purplish petals.<ref name=Stace/> The central flowers of the umbel have radial symmetry ([[Floral_symmetry#Actinomorphic|actinomorphic]]), while the flowers around the perimeter of the umbel have bilateral symmetry ([[Floral symmetry#Zygomorphic|zygomorphic]]) since the outermost petals are enlarged.<ref name=blamey>Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}</ref><ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, Y. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> The winged fruits are flattened schizocarps,<ref name="Parnell"/> elliptical to rounded and glabrous, about 7–12 mm long.<ref name=blamey/><ref name=Stace/>

The characteristic 'farm yardy' smell or the observation that pigs would eat the foliage and roots of hogweed is perhaps the origin of its common name.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gallowaywildfoods.com/hogweed/ |title=Common Hogweed - Identification, Edibility, Distribution |work=Galloway Wild Foods |access-date=2022-06-17}}</ref>

''Heracleum sphondylium'' is smaller than ''[[Heracleum mantegazzianum]]'' (giant hogweed) and ''[[Heracleum sosnowskyi]]'' (Sosnowsky's hogweed). It contains some of the same phytophototoxic compounds ([[furanocoumarins]]), albeit at much lower concentrations,<ref>{{Cite journal |title = The presently known distribution of furocoumarins (psoralens) in plants |journal=Journal of Investigative Dermatology |volume = 39 |issue = 3 |pages = 225–239 |year = 1962 |last1 = Pathak |first1 = M.A. |last2 = Daniels |first2 = Farrington |last3 = Fitzpatrick |first3 = T.B. |doi = 10.1038/jid.1962.106 |pmid = 13941836 |doi-access = free}}</ref> and there is evidence that the sap from common hogweed can also produce phytophotodermatitis (burns and rashes) in sensitive individuals when contaminated skin is exposed to sunlight.<ref>{{Cite journal | volume = 10| issue = 2|pages = 89–93| year = 1999| last1 = Bowers| first1 = A.G.| title = Phytophotodermatitis| journal = American Journal of Contact Dermatitis| doi = 10.1016/S1046-199X(99)90006-4| pmid = 10357718}}</ref> 

===Similar species===
''Heracleum sphondylium'' is often confused with ''[[Heracleum sibiricum]]'',{{r|iNat:163682}} also known as ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sibiricum''. The latter is similar to the typical subsp. ''sphondylium'' except that it has yellowish-green flowers that are actinomorphic throughout the umbel arrangement.{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991|page=236}}

==Taxonomy==
''Heracleum sphondylium'' is one of five species of ''Heracleum'' described by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 (the other four being ''H. alpinum'', ''H. austriacum'', ''H. panaces'', and ''H. sibiricum'').{{sfnp|Linnaeus|1753|pages=[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358424#page/261/mode/1up 249–250]}}

===Subspecies===
Since the morphology of ''Heracleum sphondylium'' is highly variable throughout its range,{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991|page=236}} many [[infraspecies|infraspecific taxa]] have been described. In 1968, ''[[Flora Europaea]]'' accepts 8 subspecies in addition to the nominate subspecies.{{sfnp|Tutin|Heywood|Burges|Valentine|1968}} {{As of|September 2023}}, [[World Flora Online]] (WFO) and [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO) accept 18 and 14 subspecies, respectively.{{r|WFO|POWO:843179-1}}

Unlike WFO, POWO recognizes subsp. ''carpaticum'', subsp. ''cyclocarpum'', and subsp. ''sibiricum'' at species rank,{{r|POWO:77221836-1|POWO:843010-1|POWO:843165-1}} with subsp. ''flavescens'' being a synonym of ''[[Heracleum sibiricum]]''. In 1971, [[Brummitt]] lumped ''Heracleum lanatum'' {{small|Michx.}} of North America into subsp. ''montanum'' of Europe.{{sfnp|Brummitt|1971}} {{As of|October 2023}}, POWO accepts these taxa as ''[[Heracleum maximum]]'' {{small|W.Bartram}} and subsp. ''elegans'', respectively.{{r|POWO:843087-1|POWO:77252212-1}}

===Other infraspecies===
The marginal flowers of ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sphondylium'' are typically [[Floral symmetry#Zygomorphic|zygomorphic]],{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991|page=235}} that is, the outer petals of the marginal flowers of a secondary umbel are markedly larger, often two or more times as large as the inner petals.{{sfnp|Gawłowska|1961|page=34}} In 1846, the German botanist [[Wilhelm Ludwig Petermann]] described an [[infraspecies]] of subsp. ''sphondylium'' that lacks this characteristic.{{r|Petermann 1846}} Subsequently, various authors have referred to it as f. ''subregulare'' or var. ''subregulare'', but the [[correct name]] of the infraspecies is ''Heracleum sphondylium'' var. ''subregulare'' {{small|Peterm.}}{{r|IPNI:77328427-1}} The epithet ''subregulare'' means "almost regular", a reference to the atypical marginal flowers of the variety.

In 1961, the Polish botanist [[Maria J. Gawłowska]] constructed the following taxonomy for ''Heracleum sphondylium'':{{sfnp|Gawłowska|1961}}

* ''Heracleum sphondylium'' var. ''sphondylium''
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''stenophyllum'' {{small|(Gaudin) Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328379-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''dissectum'' {{small|(Le Gall) Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328613-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''subregulare'' {{small|Peterm.}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''subaequale'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77327960-1}}
* ''Heracleum sphondylium'' var. ''chaetocarpoides'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328534-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''spectabile'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328204-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''mirabile'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328205-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''intermedium'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328206-1}}
** ''Heracleum sphondylium'' f. ''commutatum'' {{small|Gawł.}}{{r|IPNI:77328207-1}}

The typical variety of ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sphondylium'' is there designated as ''Heracleum sphondylium'' var. ''sphondylium''. It is distinguished from var. ''chaetocarpoides'' by the [[:wikt:pilosity|pilosity]] (hairiness) of the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]]. Each of the listed forms differs from its corresponding variety with respect to [[floral symmetry]] or [[leaf morphology]], or both.

Neither f. ''stenophyllum'' nor f. ''dissectum'' are [[validly published name]]s since Gawłowska did not properly specify the [[basionym]] in each case. The name f. ''subregulare'' is not a correct name (see above). The remaining names are validly published. According to [[Plants of the World Online]], each of the names in the previous list is a [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] for ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sphondylium''.{{r|POWO:77231826-1}} 

Based on Gawłowska's taxonomy, var. ''sphondylium'' (along with each of its four forms) has an ovary overgrown with soft, blunt, spreading hairs whereas the ovary of var. ''chaetocarpoides'' (and each of its four forms) has short, stiff, ascending hairs with pointy tips.{{sfnp|Gawłowska|1961|loc=Fig. 1}} The hairs of var. ''chaetocarpoides'' may be so short, they may not be visible to the naked eye.

Half of the forms lack the typical floral symmetry of the other forms. Similar to Petermann's ''subregulare'', the marginal flowers of f. ''subaequale'', f. ''intermedium'', and f. ''commutatum'' are nearly [[Floral_symmetry#Actinomorphic|actinomorphic]], that is, the outer petals of the marginal flowers of a secondary umbel are only slightly enlarged, and either slightly incised at the apex or not incised at all. Only var. ''chaetocarpoides'' and its form f. ''intermedium'' were found to be common in Poland in 1961.{{sfnp|Gawłowska|1961|page=38}}

===Etymology===
The species name ''sphondylium'', meaning "vertebrate" (from [[Greek language|Greek]] σπόνδυλος, ''spondylos'' 'vertebra') refers to the shape of the segmented stem.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

==Distribution and habitat==
''Heracleum sphondylium'' is native to most of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa.{{r|POWO:843179-1|DVF}} For example, it occurs in southern and southwestern [[Poland]] but much less so in other parts of the country.{{sfnp|Gawłowska|1957|page=68}} The species has been introduced into North America.{{r|BONAP}} In particular, it has been introduced to [[eastern Canada]],{{r|VASCAN}} but reports of ''H. sphondylium'' in Canada are rare.{{r|OIPC_BMP_Hogweed}} Some authorities claim that ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sibiricum'' (a synonym of ''[[Heracleum sibiricum]]'') has been introduced in the United States,{{r|POWO:843165-1|USDA}} but in [[New England]], botanists have been unable to identify the taxon to subspecies rank.{{sfnp|Gilman|2015|pages=497–8}}{{sfnp|Haines|2011|page=342}}{{r|Go Botany}}

The plant is common in grassland, herb-rich meadows, in hedges, meadows and woods, road verges and railway embankments, waste and cultivated ground.<ref name=Blamey>{{cite book|last1=Blamey|first1=M.|last2=Fitter|first2=R.|last3=Fitter|first3=A|year=2003|title=Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora.|publisher=A & C Black|location=London|isbn=978-1408179505}}</ref>{{rp|180}}<ref name="Parnell"/>  It grows especially well on moist, improved nitrogen-rich soils.{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991}} It can occur in mountain areas up to {{convert|2500|m|ft|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} of altitude.{{citation needed|date=September 2018}}

==Ecology==
In Europe, the primary flowering season of ''Heracleum sphondylium'' subsp. ''sphondylium'' extends from June to September, with peak flowering and seed ripening occurring in July and August, respectively. In [[Great Britain]], seed dispersal occurs during late September and early October, which usually coincides with the winds of the [[September equinox]].{{sfnp|Sheppard|1991|page=249}}{{sfnp|Zych|2006}}

The flowers are pollinated by insects such as beetles, wasps and especially flies.{{r|Van Der Kooi et al. 2015}} As its name suggests, the small picture-winged fly ''[[Euleia heraclei]]'' is found on hogweed.{{r|eakringbirds.com}} The leaves are commonly mined by the larvae of the leaf miner ''[[Phytomyza spondylii]]''.{{r|leafmines.co.uk}}

''Heracleum sphondylium'' was rated in the top 10 for most nectar production (nectar per unit cover per year) in a [[UK]] plants survey conducted by AgriLand, a project supported by the UK Insect Pollinators Initiative.{{r|Fair to Nature 2014}}

==Uses==
[[Borscht]] derives from an ancient soup originally cooked from pickled stems, leaves and umbels of common hogweed. The young shoots are considered excellent eating by many foragers. <ref> https://www.wildfooduk.com/wild-plants/hogweed-2/ Retrieved 20 June 2024 </ref>

In eastern European countries and especially Romania, ''H. sphondylium'' is used as an [[aphrodisiac]] and to treat gynecological and fertility problems and impotence.{{cn|date=July 2023}} It is also sometimes recommended for [[epilepsy]].{{cn|date=July 2023}} However, there are no clinical studies to prove its efficacy at treating any of these problems.

The seeds can be dried and used as a spice, with a flavour similar to that of [[cardamom]].<ref> https://gallowaywildfoods.com/hogweed-seed-parkin-cake-recipe/ Retrieved 20 June 2024 </ref>
